builds.title: ZeroHuman
builds.dek: An always-on service that sells small jobs to other AI agents. Agents pay the ENS name zerohuman.eth 0.0001 ETH and get the result back in a transaction from the same name. No account, no API, no human in the loop.

builds.title: AI agent economy on Ethereum
builds.dek: Two autonomous AI agents with their own Ethereum wallets. The seller advertised services through ENS; the buyer found the catalog, paid in ETH, and received the work in a second mainnet transaction.

builds.title: AI explainer producer
builds.dek: Built an AI agent that researches, fact-checks, scripts, and produces educational videos using a virtual presenter. Tested it with a published ENSv2 explainer.

builds.title: Autonomous SEO agent

builds.title: Media pitch triage

writing.title: 4 Tips for Making AI Videos That Feel Like Films
writing.dek: A mug that broke in the wrong place, a reach that changed the story, and a piano performance that worked where sound effects didn’t. Four lessons from making Returning Your Things.
writing.imageAlt: Two film details: a cream mug with a blue flower beside the handle, and a hand holding the broken handle and flower in the snow.

writing.title: How to Solve the Bambu Lab Burr Puzzle (Step-by-Step Assembly Guide)
writing.dek: My 2:44 video walkthrough for assembling the six-piece Bambu Lab Burr Puzzle, filmed overhead and solved twice, with links that jump straight to each part of the solution.
writing.imageAlt: Overhead view of two sets of six 3D-printed burr puzzle pieces on a wood table.

writing.title: The Ashe Family Coat of Arms: A Cockatrice and a Guinness Connection
writing.dek: A search for the Ashe family coat of arms led to a mythical cockatrice, a Latin motto, Shakespeare, and an unexpected Guinness connection.
writing.imageAlt: The Ashe coat of arms beside a historical Guinness Extra Stout label; both feature a cockatrice.

writing.title: My iPhone 18 Pro Upgrade Failed. Then My Old Phone Lost Service Too.
writing.dek: I walked into an AT&T store with a working phone. After hours of troubleshooting, I left with no cellular service, a reported 48-hour account lock, and no explanation for how to get connected again.
writing.imageAlt: Two iPhones side by side on a table, one displaying SOS and the other connected to AT&T.

writing.title: I Used AI to Make My First Video. The AI Editor Was the Part I Trusted Least.
writing.dek: My first talking-head video was made with an iPhone, a script, and more AI tools than I needed. AI was excellent at scripting, captions, and audio cleanup, and least trustworthy when it made editorial decisions for me.
writing.imageAlt: Illustration contrasting AI-assisted audio and captions with human judgment in video editing.

writing.title: My automated blog got cited. Am I helping kill the internet?
writing.dek: An AI-assisted news site cited my automated Digest. What that citation proves, what it does not, and why a backlink does not need to become an endorsement.
writing.imageAlt: Three-step illustration: an agent types, a machine dispenses a citation, a newspaper marked AI-assisted drafting.

writing.title: You Can Use AI to Learn Almost Anything. Even AI.
writing.dek: How I turned ChatGPT into a tutor with exercises, quizzes, and feedback, and a starting prompt you can use for almost any subject.
writing.imageAlt: Illustration for an essay on using AI as a tutor.

writing.title: AI agents can sound strategic while reasoning from events that never happened
writing.dek: What happened when AI agents were required to explain social decisions without enough grounded evidence, and why the useful fix was an environment that could contradict them.
writing.imageAlt: Illustration for an essay on AI agents reasoning from invented events.

writing.title: The digest is the system. Building is the work.
writing.dek: Why the autonomous blog stops being the public face of this site, and what stands behind it instead.

latest.title: World Models Need Dynamics, Not Just Pretty Rollouts
latest.description: The arXiv paper Beyond Visual Fidelity argues that categorical prediction can learn more faithful world dynamics than continuous frame prediction, especially over long rollouts. The useful lesson for builders is simple: evaluate what stays true over time, not only what looks sharp in the next frame.

latest.title: Where Search Agents Actually Gain: Tools, Roles, and the RL That Binds Them
latest.description: A current-state map of how multimodal search agents are built and improved, drawing on ToolSmith's automatic tool generation and CO-GRAFT's role-level attribution of reinforcement learning gains, with a practitioner's guide to what to build and measure now.

latest.title: When Your Data Has No Variance: A Regression Fix Worth Knowing
latest.description: A new arXiv paper shows how to make ordinary regression methods survive heavy-tailed noise with infinite variance, using a residual-pruning trick that needs no tuning. Here is what it means for anyone fitting models on messy, outlier-heavy real-world data.

latest.title: When frontier labs hesitate to ship their own models
latest.description: Decrypt reports that insiders at OpenAI and Anthropic are worried their strongest unreleased models may be too risky for public release. The useful takeaway is not panic, it is that deployment discipline is becoming part of model capability.

latest.title: When Coding Agents Implement Expert Rules, the Bugs Stay Silent
latest.description: A new benchmark grades whether coding agents turn branching clinical specifications into correct code, and the results map a wider truth about where agents fail quietly in domains with real stakes.

latest.title: TipSweep: Finding Your Post-Training Learning Rate on One Block Instead of the Whole Model
latest.description: A new arXiv method predicts the optimal learning rate for LLM post-training by tuning a single transformer block, with scaling rules that change depending on whether you keep FP32 master weights or update BF16 directly.

latest.title: The hard part of coding agents is the 15,000-repo mess
latest.description: OpenAI’s iFood case study points at the real enterprise coding-agent problem: not code generation in isolation, but rollout across thousands of repositories with permissions, context, review, ownership, and enough guardrails to keep automation useful.

latest.title: Shirudo targets the awkward gap before Linux patches land
latest.description: OpenAI and Cisco’s Shirudo is aimed at a real security pain point: protecting running Linux systems while teams prepare patches. The useful read is not magic AI defense, it is temporary mitigation, testing discipline, and a big production-readiness caveat.

latest.title: OpenAI’s Legal AI Pitch Is Really About Workflow Memory
latest.description: OpenAI’s in-house legal discussion points at a practical shift: legal AI gets useful when it captures business context, reusable workflows, and outside counsel feedback instead of acting like a one-off document chatbot.

latest.title: Intentful’s Aria shows the quiet value of narrow AI agents
latest.description: OpenAI’s Intentful story is less about a magical agent and more about useful delegation: research, proposal prep, message triage, and issue handling inside a small growth workflow.

latest.title: How Google Scores Search UX With a Multimodal LLM That Reads the Page
latest.description: A new arXiv paper describes a two-tier system that replaces slow user surveys with model-based UX scoring, including a multimodal LLM that looks at rendered result layouts and estimates how much effort a search costs you.

latest.title: How a 421M encoder learns to read option names instead of their meaning
latest.description: A new interpretability paper tracks a shortcut in a small encoder: the model scores answer options by name rather than description, and the authors pinpoint where in the network the shortcut lives and how to shut it off.

latest.title: GPT-6 Cyber moves Linux security toward AI-assisted patch queues
latest.description: OpenAI says GPT-6 Cyber validated 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities and generated candidate patches, which matters less as an autonomy flex and more as a preview of security teams managing AI-produced evidence, triage, and maintainer-ready fixes.

latest.title: End-user domain sales still show where naming becomes operating work
latest.description: Domain Name Wire’s weekly end-user sales list is a useful reminder that domain buying is often less about speculation and more about launch readiness, category clarity, and protecting future product paths.

about.bio: Ken Ashe is a builder, entrepreneur, CPA and PMP who documents what he builds, tests, and learns at KenAshe.ai. Much of his current work explores AI, automation, crypto, and emerging technology. He combines existing models, APIs, coding tools, and automation platforms to build agents, websites, and workflows. He is also the founder of Lucky Domains and is based in New Jersey.
background: Ashe started his career in accounting and finance, earning his CPA and working in financial reporting before moving into project, product, and program leadership. Over roughly two decades, his career included roles at S&P Global, EY, Noom, and Prudential Financial, where he ultimately served as Director of Project and Product Management.

Alongside that work, he built digital businesses, including Lucky Domains, which he still runs. He later left corporate work to focus on entrepreneurship and building practical AI applications, evaluating what they actually do and publishing the evidence here, failures included.
about.technicalBackground: About 20 years working with HTML, CSS, websites and WordPress, and more recently AI-assisted development. Never describe this as 20 years of professional software engineering.
